native_result.query: How is the advantage in BA degree completion rates for Black students related to Socioeconomic status levels?
native_result.HypoA: The advantage in BA degree completion rates for Black students is more pronounced at lower SES levels with the interaction term for Socioeconomic status and being black having a coefficient of 0.7606
native_result.HypoB: The literal BA-degree-completion-rate framing cannot be answered from this dataset (the supplied flat file contains a single respondent-education snapshot, dated 1979, when respondents are 14–22; only ~38 of 12,686 records have grade ≥ 16). We therefore use a faithful reframe — post-secondary access by 1979 (grade ≥ 13) — and ask how the Black–NBNH gap in that outcome is related to socioeconomic status. The answer is: (a) there is no Black advantage at any SES level — Black rates are lower than NBNH at every tertile; (b) descriptively the Black–NBNH gap is largest in magnitude at the LOWEST SES tertile (−11.5 pp, rate ratio 0.57, 95% CI [0.43, 0.74]); and (c) the formal Wald test of the two race × SES interactions in a logistic model adjusted for sex, age, and max parental grade is not statistically significant (χ²(2) = 0.83, p = 0.66). The same covariate-adjusted model, when used to predict probabilities at sample-mean covariate values (i.e., holding max parental grade at the pooled sample mean while varying SES), predicts Black > NBNH at every SES tertile (20.3% vs. 16.6% at low SES, etc.) — the opposite direction from the descriptive rates and an apparent contradiction that would mislead a reader who saw only the prediction table. This counterfactual reversal is a Simpson-style artifact of holding parental education constant at the pooled mean: the z-composite SES sensitivity, which absorbs parental education directly into the SES construct, collapses the Black–NBNH gap to near zero and statistically indistinguishable from zero at every tertile (+0.6, +2.2, −0.9 pp; all 95% CIs include zero), confirming parental education — not contemporaneous family income — as the dominant channel through which the racial gap operates. Together these results support the descriptive-negative / moderation-not-significant reading as the substantively supported one: the question's presupposition of a Black advantage is not supported in this 1979 baseline of NLSY79, the disparity is negative throughout and most adverse for Black students at low SES, and the formal moderation by SES is not statistically detectable at this sample size. Sensitivity checks at the grade ≥ 15 cut-off preserve the negative sign of the gap and the 'gap largest at low SES' pattern; switching SES to a wealth-1985 tertile shifts the largest gap to HIGH SES (−12.0 pp), confirming that the precise SES tertile hosting the largest disparity is sensitive to how SES is operationalized while the sign of the gap (Black ≤ NBNH) is robust.
native_result.WorkflowB: Loaded data/nls_raw.csv (12,686 × 61, columns match docs 1:1; grade=95 dropped). Restricted to age 18–22 (N=7,104). Primary SES = log(family_income_1979 + 1) tertiled in the analytic sample; sensitivities = log(family_net_wealth_1985) tertiled and a z-composite (log-income + max-parent-grade + −family-size). Outcome = grade in [Highest grade completed, 1979] ≥ 13 (primary); ≥ 15 (sensitivity); ≥ 16 (caveat cell only). Computed race × SES crosstabs for Black vs. NBNH (reference) with signed Black−NBNH rate differences (normal-approx 95% CI, 2,000-iteration percentile bootstrap CI) and rate ratios with log-normal 95% CI. Hispanic arm reported as a compact standalone table (not pooled into the reference). Logistic regression of any_coll_13 on is_black + ses_mid + ses_high + is_black × ses_mid + is_black × ses_high + female + age_1979 (centered) + max_parent_grade, with HC1 robust SE; Wald test on the two race × SES interactions. Average marginal effects computed for each race. Robustness: Poisson regression with robust SE on the same design matrix; rate-ratio analogues reported. Complete-case analysis; no survey weights (file does not include them); MAR assumption noted. The apparent Simpson-style contradiction between descriptive rates (Black < NBNH at every SES) and covariate-standardized predictions (Black > NBNH at every SES) is documented; the z-composite SES sensitivity collapses the gap to near zero, identifying parental education as the channel through which the racial gap operates.
